content.title: Yaxel Lendeborg’s driving force, his mother, now fights her own battle
content.text: Wolverines BasketballMichigan Wolverines forward Yaxel Lendeborg (23) celebrates during practice day before the Final Four at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis on Friday, April 3 2026.MLive.comBy Andrew Kahn | akahn1@mlive.comINDIANAPOLIS — Yaxel Lendeborg’s mom has become an NCAA Tournament star, appearing on TV often as her son has led Michigan to the Final Four.Despite a cancer diagnosis, Yissel Raposo will be at Lucas Oil Stadium on Saturday night when Michigan plays Arizona (approximately 8:50 p.m. ET, TBS).Raposo is the reason Lendeborg is here. She forced him to take classes away from his high school to get his grades in order. She made him get on a plane, against his will, and enroll at a junior college in Arizona. After three years at Arizona Western and two at UAB, Lendeborg has made his lone season as Michigan memorable. He is the Big Ten Player of the Year and is averaging 21 points and 7.3 rebounds during Michigan’s NCAA Tournament run.Throughout it all, he’s mentioned his mom.“None of this would be possible if it wasn’t for her helping me out and believing in me more than I believed in myself,” Lendeborg said earlier in this Tournament. “The majority of the times when she’s here and she’s in the stands, I get a lot more aggressive. She has this certain calling that she does whenever I get the ball. I can hear nobody else in the stadium but her. It puts me in attack mode, honestly.”In February, Lendeborg penned a piece for The Players’ Tribune in which he revealed his mom had cancer.“She said she had kept it from me, and didn’t want to say anything, because she knew how important this season was for me, and she didn’t want to mess it up,” Lendeborg wrote. “Didn’t want to do anything to jeopardize my future. It was so sad, man. But it says so much. She finds out she has cancer, and … she’s thinking about me.”Raposo has Stage 4 appendix cancer, she said in a phone interview Friday. She was on her way to the airport, heading to Indianapolis to watch Michigan. She has had 11 chemotherapy treatments and will have a 12th, after which she might undergo radiation and eventually surgery.She often feels tired but when she has the energy she is in the stands at Michigan games. “I’m alive,” she said. “That’s the good thing.”Lendeborg was driving when she broke the news. “He stopped the car and started crying a lot,” she said. “I was crying a lot too. I told him how to be strong and told him I was going to be OK.”Like many parents, Raposo — who was a college basketball and volleyball player in Puerto Rico when Lendeborg was born — had not heard her son express the feelings he has at press conferences and in his written story.“I’m surprised that he told all this about me, about when he was little,” Raposo said. “I’m surprised, but I’m happy at the same time.”451/45Michigan practices in Indianapolis before Final Four on Saturday, April 3 2026.‘We shocked the world.
